analysis.one_liner: Removes federal criminal penalties for marijuana and regulates it like tobacco with a legal purchase age of 21.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than a committee referral: introduced on July 30, 2020 with no cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended in January 2021, and marijuana remained a Schedule I controlled substance.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take marijuana out of the most restrictive category of federal drug law, erasing it from the list of Schedule I substances alongside heroin. The change would apply retroactively, so past and pending federal marijuana cases and convictions could be wiped out, including cases against juveniles. In place of prohibition, the FDA would regulate cannabis products the way it regulates tobacco, with a federal ban on selling to anyone under 21, plus Agriculture Department quality rules, customs rules for imports and exports, easier federal funding for cannabis medical research, a national youth-use prevention strategy, and research on detecting cannabis-impaired driving that must be checked for racial bias.
analysis.who_benefits: People with federal marijuana convictions or pending federal cases, including juveniles, because the decriminalization is written to apply retroactively to offenses committed before the bill's enactment [S2][S3]. Adults under 21 and anyone who would no longer face federal arrest for cannabis possession would also benefit [S2]. Because the bill requires federal agencies to assess whether enforcement tools would have racially disparate impacts, communities that have borne the brunt of marijuana enforcement stand to gain the most [S2][S3]. Researchers would benefit from a ban on rejecting grant applications solely because the study involves cannabis [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes marijuana and THC from the Schedule I list of controlled substances and strikes marijuana from various federal criminal provisions, with the removal retroactive to pending and past cases and convictions, including juvenile adjudications [S2][S3].

Directs the FDA to regulate cannabis products the same way it regulates tobacco, including labeling and advertising rules, and makes it illegal for any retailer to sell cannabis to anyone under 21 [S2][S3].

Requires national research institutes to consider cannabis-related medical research applications on the same basis as any other application and bars rejecting a grant solely because it involves cannabis [S2][S3].

Requires a national youth cannabis-abuse prevention strategy and federal research on detecting cannabis-impaired driving, with both required to assess and guard against racially disparate impacts, and directs the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to publish its findings and its reasons for adopting or rejecting each method [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal drug enforcement agencies lose the cannabis caseload that generates arrests, prosecutions, and seizures, since the bill strikes marijuana from the criminal provisions those agencies enforce [S2][S3]. Cannabis businesses would take on compliance costs under tobacco-style FDA labeling, advertising, and age-verification rules, and the FDA, USDA, and Customs and Border Protection would absorb new regulatory workloads [S2][S3]. Anyone who favors keeping marijuana illegal on public-health grounds bears the cost of a fully legal commercial market, since the bill applies tobacco-style regulation, a regime under which tobacco products have remained widely sold, rather than a stricter pharmaceutical model [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug enforcement agencies and cannabis sellers

drawbacks.text: The FDA would regulate cannabis the way it regulates tobacco, which is one of the weaker regulatory regimes: tobacco products remain broadly on the market under grandfathering rather than undergoing pre-market approval, so a legal cannabis market could look commercially much like the existing state-level pot industry rather than a tightly controlled pharmaceutical product [S2][S3].

Legalization would create a large legal commercial market before reliable methods exist for detecting cannabis-impaired driving; the bill only requires research on such methods and publication of results, not a working enforcement standard [S2][S3].

Retroactively erasing federal convictions and juvenile adjudications is sweeping and would apply to cases entered before enactment, which supporters framed as relief from unequal enforcement but which opponents would weigh against the seriousness of some underlying conduct [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs full federal decriminalization, including retroactive relief for people already convicted, with a regulated legal market, which addresses the main objection that legalization would simply open an unregulated free-for-all. The honest cost is that tobacco-style regulation is a light-touch model, impaired-driving detection would lag behind legalization, and the bill leaves states to handle whatever local rules they choose. Weighing the removal of criminal penalties, including for juveniles, against the enforcement gap, the design is reasonable, and the bill failed for lack of support rather than because of a legislative flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 30, 2020 and read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the Substance Regulation and Safety Act of 2020 on July 30, 2020, and no other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and that referral was the last action on the bill in the 116th Congress [S1][S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, so marijuana remained a Schedule I controlled substance when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S2][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal marijuana prohibition stayed intact, so the enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and prison and surveillance systems whose caseloads depend on cannabis being illegal were no worse off, and anyone whose convictions would have been erased gained nothing. The status quo also preserved the state-by-state patchwork that existing licensed cannabis operators already navigate.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota and the bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 30, 2020; it was her only listed action besides the referral [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: The committee of referral, chaired by Lindsey Graham (R-SC) during the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 30, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.role: Senate Majority Leader in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills got Senate floor time, and the bill never received floor action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's single sponsor was a Democrat, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and it died in a committee controlled by Republicans [S4][S5].

industries.note: Full federal descheduling would legalize what is now a federally illegal product, opening interstate commerce, banking access, and import/export channels for cannabis companies [S2][S3]. Ordinary consumers gain alongside them from decriminalization, though tobacco-style FDA rules, a hard age-21 floor, and USDA quality regulations would impose real compliance costs on the industry [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Drug enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and the prison and drug-testing apparatus
industries.note: The bill strikes marijuana from the controlled-substances schedules and from the criminal provisions, wiretap authorities, and forest-drug-control laws that generate arrests, prosecutions, and seizures [S2][S3]. The industry's loss is the public's gain in the form of no more federal cannabis arrests, with the losses falling hardest on people already convicted before enactment only if relief is applied.
